paragraphs.text: Many linguists predict that at least half the world's 6,000 or so languages will be dead or dying by the year 2050. Languages are becoming extinct at twice the rate of endangered mammals and four times the rate of endangered birds. If this trend continues, the world of the future could be dominated by a dozen or fewer languages. Michael Krauss, director of the Alaska Native Language Center, suggests that as many as 90 per cent of languages could be dying or extinct by 2100. According to Krauss, 20 to 40 per cent of languages are already declining, and only 5 to 10 per cent are 'safe' in the sense of being widely spoken or having official status. If people 'become wise and turn it around', Krauss says, the number of dead or dying languages could perhaps be 50 per cent by 2100.

The definition of a healthy language is one that acquires new speakers. No matter how many adults use the language, if it isn't passed to the next generation, its future as a living language is in jeopardy. A language may continue to exist for a long time as a second or ceremonial language, but it is on the way out as soon as children stop learning it. Although language extinction is sad for the people involved, why should the rest of us care? Replacing a minor language with a more widespread one may even seem like a good thing, allowing people to communicate with each other more easily. But it isn't. Language diversity is as important as biological diversity.

Andrew Woodfield, director of the Centre for Theories of Language and Learning in Bristol, England, suggested in a seminar on language conservation that people do not know 'exactly what riches are hidden inside the less-studied languages'. Woodfield compares one argument for conserving unstudied endangered plants — that they may be medically valuable —with the argument for conserving endangered languages. 'We have inductive evidence based on past studies of well-known languages that there will be riches, even though we do not know what they will be. By allowing languages to die out, the human race is destroying things it doesn't understand,' he argues.

Stephen Wurm, in 'The World's Languages in Danger', tells the story of one medical cure that depended on knowledge of a traditional language. In Northern Australia there was an outbreak of severe skin ulcers that resisted conventional treatment. Aborigines, descendants of the original inhabitants of Australia, who were acquainted with a nurse working on the case, told her about a lotion derived from a local medicinal plant. The lotion healed the ulcers. This incident and similar ones have resulted in a general search for medicinal plants known to aboriginal people through their languages and traditional cultures. Most Australian languages are dying. When they go, the medical knowledge stored in them will go, too.

As Krauss aptly expresses it, the web of languages is a 'microcosm of highly specialized information. Every language has its own take on the world. One language is not simply a different set of words for the same things.' He further argues that just as we depend on biological complexity for our physical survival, we depend on linguistic complexity for our cultural survival.

Some language loss, like species loss, is natural and predictable. Just as plants and animals have appeared and disappeared over the millennia, languages evolve, grow, spread, and eventually dwindle and die. Sometimes they're replaced by their 'descendant' languages, as Italian gradually replaced Latin in Europe. Other times they're forced out, as the ancient Etruscan language was when Latin speakers overran the Italian peninsula.

Language extinction is accelerating today for some of the same reasons as species extinction — population pressures and the spread of industrialization. The global economy often forces small, unindustrialized communities to choose between their traditional language and participation in the larger world. Sometimes more global languages coexist with the local language. More often, they eventually replace it as older speakers die and younger ones adopt the more useful tongue. Even strong national languages have some worries. The European Union, for instance, is increasingly concerned that English will eventually replace some European languages, since it's the only language many Europeans have in common.

The deck is stacked heavily against the world's minority languages, but the case isn't hopeless. We've seen that, with effort, plants and animals can be brought back from the edge of extinction. Languages, too, can be turned around.

The Cornish language, once spoken in southwestern England, expired in 1777 when its last living speaker died, but has made a comeback. With the help of surviving documents, a small group of descendants of Cornish speakers began to learn their language and speak it to their children. Now, about 2,000 people speak Cornish. Other examples of resuscitated languages are Welsh and Navajo. Speakers revitalized their dying languages through 'immersion' high schools where students use their ancestral language every day. Both languages have grown in numbers of speakers over the past few decades.

The Native California Network is a program that teams fluent speakers of native Californian languages with apprentice speakers. The apprentices immerse themselves in conversations with the 'master' speakers and meet with groups for weekly conversation. It has had an effect. Speakers of one native Californian language, Hupa, for instance, have succeeded in getting Hupa to count as a foreign language for college entrance requirements. Even a few such language apprenticeships may help avert the wholesale extinction of minor languages.

content: Through various efforts, some languages have been brought back from the brink of extinction. Two examples are Welsh and Navajo. In these cases, {{33}} are immersed in the language every day. A programme in California matches novice speakers with fluent speakers of native languages and there is now {{34}} for one of these languages. Similarly, a group of learners in southwestern England have used {{35}} to help them bring the language of their Cornish ancestors back to life.
